## Question 1: Implementing K-means

K-means is a relatively simple algorithm that we can write ourselves. For Questions 1 and 2, do not use an existing function that performs K-means directly.

Generate 10 observations with two independent standard normal coordinates. Set a random seed and report it. Randomly assign the observations to $K=2$ clusters, making sure neither cluster is empty. Let $C(i)$ denote the cluster assigned to observation $x_i$, and let $m_k$ denote the mean of cluster $k$.

a.  Perform one iteration: calculate the cluster means, then assign each observation to its closest mean using Euclidean distance. Report the means and updated assignments, and plot the observations colored by their updated assignments.

    ```{r}
    # Source: Week 11 Lecture: K-Means
    set.seed(43201)
    print("The seed is 43201.")

    # Generate 10 observations with two independent standard normal coordinates
    data <- matrix(rnorm(n = 20, mean = 0, sd = 1), nrow = 10, ncol = 2)

    # Randomly assign points into clusters 1 or 2
    # Use C(i) to denote the clusters; make sure neither cluster is empty
    C <- sample(1:2, size = 10, replace = TRUE)
    while(sum(C == 1) == 0 | sum(C == 2) == 0){
      C <- sample(1:2, size = 10, replace = TRUE)
    }

    # Calculate cluster means
    m1 <- colMeans(data[C == 1, , drop = FALSE])
    m2 <- colMeans(data[C == 2, , drop = FALSE])
    mk <- rbind(m1, m2)

    # Calculate the distances between the observations and the cluster means
    # MARGIN = 2 means to apply the fuction to each column
    # sweep subtracts mean coordinates from columns and squares the differences
    # rowSums adds the x1 and x2 coordinates together per observation
    distances <- sapply(1:2, function(k){
      sqrt(rowSums(sweep(data, MARGIN = 2, mk[k, ])^2))
    })

    # Assign each observation to its closest mean using Euclidean distance
    # MARGIN = 1 means to apply the function to each row
    C <- apply(distances, MARGIN = 1, which.min)

    # Report means and updated assignments
    mk
    C

    # Plot observations colored by their updated assignments
    cluster_colors <- c("deepskyblue", "darkorange")
    plot(data,
         main = "First Iteration of K-means", xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
         pch = 19, 
         cex = 1,
         col = cluster_colors[C])
    points(mk, pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 3, col = cluster_colors)
    ```

b.  Write a function that repeats these two steps until the assignments stop changing or a specified maximum number of iterations is reached. Your function should work for a data matrix with any number of variables and a chosen number of clusters $K$. Start from a nonempty assignment to each cluster; if a cluster becomes empty during iteration, keep its previous mean. Recalculate the cluster means from the final assignments before returning them. Return the final assignments, cluster means, and within-cluster sum of squares,

    $$
    \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i:\,C(i)=k}\lVert x_i-m_k\rVert^2.
    $$

    ```{r}
    set.seed(43201)
    k_means <- function(x, k, max_iter){
      n <- nrow(x)
      
      # Initialize setup
      # Randomly assign points into clusters k
      # Redraw until every cluster has at least one point
      C <- sample(1:k, size = n, replace = TRUE)
      while(any(tabulate(C, nbins = k) == 0)){
        C <- sample(1:k, size = n, replace = TRUE)
      }
      
      mk <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = k, ncol = ncol(x))
      
      for (iter in seq_len(max_iter)){
        
        old_C <- C
        
        # Count how many observations are assigned to each cluster
        cluster_sizes <- tabulate(C, nbins = k)
        empty_clusters <- which(cluster_sizes == 0)
        
        # Calculate cluster means
        # If a cluster becomes empty during iteration, keep its previous mean
        for (i in seq_len(k)){
          if (cluster_sizes[i] > 0){
            mk[i, ] <- colMeans(x[C == i, , drop = FALSE])
          }
        }
        
        # Calculate the distances between the observations and the cluster means
        distances <- sapply(seq_len(k), function(i){
          rowSums(sweep(x, MARGIN = 2, mk[i, ])^2)
        })
        
        # Assign each observation to its closest mean using Euclidean distance
        C <- apply(distances, MARGIN = 1, which.min)
         
        # Check if assignments stopped changing
        if (all(C == old_C)){
          break
        }
      }
      
      # Recalculate means from final assignments
      cluster_sizes <- tabulate(C, nbins = k)
      for (i in seq_len(k)){
        if (cluster_sizes[i] > 0){
          mk[i, ] <- colMeans(x[C == i, , drop = FALSE])
        }
      }
      
      # Calculate witihn-cluster sums of squares
      within_cluster_ss <- sum(rowSums((x - mk[C, , drop = FALSE])^2))
      
      # Report final assignments, cluster means, and within-cluster sums of squares
      return(list(
        assignments = C,
        means = mk,
        within_cluster_ss = within_cluster_ss
      ))
      
    }
    ```

c.  Apply your function to the same 10 observations from two different random initial assignments. Report the final plots, cluster means, and within-cluster sums of squares. Do the two runs produce the same grouping and objective value? Explain your findings.

    ```{r}
    results1 <- k_means(data, k = 2, max_iter = 100)
    results1

    results2 <- k_means(data, k = 2, max_iter = 100)
    results2

    # Plot observations colored by their updated assignments
    plot(data,
         main = "K-means", xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
         pch = 19, 
         cex = 1,
         col = cluster_colors[C])
    points(results1$means, pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 3, col = cluster_colors)

    plot(data,
         main = "K-means", xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
         pch = 19, 
         cex = 1,
         col = cluster_colors[C])
    points(results2$means, pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 3, col = cluster_colors)
    ```

    Sometimes, the two runs produce the same groupings, means, and within-clusters sums of squares after 100 iterations. In addition, the label (or colors) of the group means are flipped if the code chunk is ran again. Both initializations reached the same grouping and objective value.

    If the code chunk was run again, the two runs may produce the same groupings but different means and within-clusters sums of squares. This could possibly be due to the function finding the local minimum for each iteration.

## Question 2: Image color compression

Pick your favorite color image and use your K-means function from Question 1 to cluster its pixels. For computational efficiency, resize the image to no more than $200\times200$ pixels and use its three RGB color channels.

a.  Plot the original image and report its dimensions. Transform it into a data matrix with one observation per pixel and three variables: red, green, and blue. Report the dimensions of this matrix.

    The original image has been plotted since the resized image is too pixelated to see clearly. Dimensions for both the original and resized images are reported.

    ```{r}
    # Source: Week 11 Lecture: K-Means
    # Import png image
    library(png)
    original_img <- readPNG("data/painted_inazuma_city_Vigamox.png")

    # Plot the original image (reszied image is too pixelated to see clearly)
    plot.new()
    plot.window(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
    rasterImage(original_img, 0, 0, 1, 1)
    dim(original_img)

    # After resizing, report its dimensions
    img <- readPNG("data/painted_inazuma_city_Vigamox_resized.png")
    dim(img)

    # Vectorize each red, green, and blue layer in column order
    img_expand <- apply(img, 3, c)
    dim(img_expand)
    ```

b.  For $K=2,3,5,10$, apply your function to the pixel data. Report the cluster means and within-cluster sum of squares for each $K$. Reconstruct and plot each compressed image by replacing every pixel with its assigned cluster mean. Use the same RGB scale for all fits.

    ```{r}
    # Apply function to pixel data
    fit1 <- k_means(img_expand, k = 2, max_iter = 100)
    fit2 <- k_means(img_expand, k = 3, max_iter = 100)
    fit3 <- k_means(img_expand, k = 5, max_iter = 100)
    fit4 <- k_means(img_expand, k = 10, max_iter = 100)

    # Report cluster means and within-cluster sum of squares for each K
    fits <- list(
      "2" = fit1,
      "3" = fit2,
      "5" = fit3,
      "10" = fit4
    )

    results_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(k){
      fit <- fits[[k]]
      
      data.frame(
        k = as.integer(k),
        cluster = seq_len(nrow(fit$means)),
        red = fit$means[, 1],
        green = fit$means[, 2],
        blue = fit$means[, 3],
        within_cluster_ss = fit$within_cluster_ss
      )
    }))

    results_table

    # Replace every pixel with its assigned cluster mean
    img_rbg <- img[, , 1:3]
    fits1 <- list(fit1, fit2, fit3, fit4)

    par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

    for (fit in fits){
      
      # Replace each pixel with the mean of its assigned cluster
      # fit$assignments gives each pixel's cluser label
      # fit$means contains the RGB mean for each cluster
      compressed_pixels <- fit$means[fit$assignments, , drop = FALSE]
      
      # Reshape the pixel rows into height x width x 3
      compressed_img <- array(compressed_pixels, dim = dim(img_rbg))
      
      # Plot each compressed image
      plot.new()
      plot.window(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
      rasterImage(compressed_img, 0, 0, 1, 1)
      title(main = paste("K = ", nrow(fit$means)))
    }
    ```

c.  Which value of $K$ would you choose for this image? Briefly justify your choice using the reconstructed images and the within-cluster sums of squares.

    I would choose $K = 10$ because the reconstructed image has more colors and shapes than the other images. The images for $K = 2$ and $K = 3$ are flat, and it is difficult to tell what the image is supposed to be. The image for $K = 5$ has more detail, but the image for $K = 10$ has more details and color variation. In addition, $K = 10$ has the lowest within-cluster sum of squares compared to the other $K$ values.

## Question 3: Hierarchical clustering of cars

a.  Standardize each numerical variable to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Using Euclidean distance, perform hierarchical clustering with single, complete, and average linkage. Plot the three dendrograms with the car names and compare the results.

    ```{r}
    # Source: Week 11 Lecture: Hierarchical Clustering
    # Load the data
    df_mtcars <- read.csv("data/mtcars.csv")
    ```

b.  Choose one linkage method and a number of clusters that you consider reasonable. Report the cluster memberships and a table of cluster means on the original variable scales. Describe the main characteristics of the groups and explain your choice using the dendrogram and table. Briefly explain why standardizing the variables matters for this analysis.
